name: PLAID (PLCG2-associated antibody deficiency and immune dysregulation)
aliases: PLCG2-associated antibody deficiency and immune dysregulation

clinicalPearls: Caused by mutations in PLCG2, which encodes phospholipase C gamma 2, a signalling enzyme important in immune cells
Characterised by cold-induced urticaria triggered by evaporative cooling rather than by contact with a cold object
Combines an autoinflammatory cold urticaria with features of humoral immunodeficiency and autoimmunity
Antibody deficiency predisposes to recurrent sinopulmonary infection and may require immunoglobulin support
Autoimmune and granulomatous manifestations, including autoantibodies, can coexist with the immunodeficiency
The cold urticaria differs from classic acquired cold urticaria and from cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes
Management is largely supportive, targeting infection risk, cold avoidance, and specific autoimmune complications
reference.pathophysiology: PLAID results from mutations in PLCG2 that alter phospholipase C gamma 2 signalling in immune cells such as B lymphocytes, natural killer cells, and mast cells. The abnormal enzyme shows enhanced activity at reduced temperatures, so mild cooling of the skin triggers mast cell activation and urticaria. The same signalling defect disturbs B-cell development and function, producing antibody deficiency alongside a paradoxical tendency to autoimmunity and, in some, granulomatous disease. This dual disturbance explains the coexistence of cold urticaria, immunodeficiency, and immune dysregulation.
additionalDifferentials: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS) with cold-triggered features
APLAID (PLCG2 autoinflammation and immune dysregulation) variant
Systemic autoimmune disease with cutaneous features
additionalInvestigations: Evaporative cooling challenge reproducing cold urticaria
Immunoglobulin levels and specific antibody responses
Lymphocyte subset analysis including B-cell subsets
Assessment for granulomatous disease where clinically suggested
redFlags: Recurrent or severe sinopulmonary infections indicating significant antibody deficiency
Anaphylaxis or airway involvement during cold exposure
Emergence of serious autoimmune or granulomatous complications
reference.prognosis: PLAID is a chronic condition; with cold avoidance, infection management, and treatment of autoimmune complications, many patients do well, though antibody deficiency and autoimmunity require ongoing care.
pitfalls: Confusing cold-evaporation urticaria with cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes and mistargeting therapy
Overlooking the underlying antibody deficiency and infection risk
Attributing autoimmunity to an unrelated primary autoimmune disease
Testing only for classic contact cold urticaria and missing the evaporative trigger
management: Avoidance of evaporative skin cooling, the principal trigger of the cold urticaria
Antihistamines to attenuate cold-induced urticarial symptoms
Immunoglobulin replacement therapy for significant antibody deficiency
Prompt treatment and, where needed, prophylaxis of recurrent sinopulmonary infections
Immunosuppressive treatment of autoimmune and granulomatous manifestations as they arise
Regular vaccination and immunological monitoring within specialist immunology care
Genetic counselling and family testing for this PLCG2-associated dominant disorder
